title: The MOS Capacitor
description: The heart of the MOSFET: band bending, accumulation, depletion and inversion, flat-band and threshold voltage, and the C–V curve.

study.title: Accumulation, depletion, inversion
study.body:
A MOS capacitor is a gate (metal or heavily doped polysilicon), a thin SiO$_2$ layer and the silicon substrate, here p-type. The gate voltage $V_G$ controls the charge at the silicon surface:
- **Accumulation** ($V_G < V_{FB}$): holes pile up at the surface.
- **Depletion** ($V_{FB} < V_G < V_T$): holes are pushed away, uncovering negative acceptors over a depth $x_d$.
- **Inversion** ($V_G > V_T$): electrons collect in a thin surface layer: the surface has become n-type. This electron layer is the MOSFET channel.

study.title: Explore: band bending
study.body: The **surface potential** $\phi_s$ is how far the bands bend down at the surface (p-type substrate, $N_a = 10^{16}$ cm⁻³, depth on the horizontal axis). $E_F$ stays flat because no current flows through the oxide. When $E_{Fi}$ at the surface drops below $E_F$, the surface is inverted; at $\phi_s = 2\phi_{fp}$ = 0.69 V the surface electron density equals the bulk hole density: **threshold**. Negative $\phi_s$ bends the bands up: accumulation.

study.title: Depletion width and threshold
study.body: In depletion the band bending is carried by a layer of ionized acceptors of depth $x_d = \sqrt{2\varepsilon_s\phi_s/qN_a}$. At threshold ($\phi_s = 2\phi_{fp}$) it reaches its maximum $x_{dT}$: beyond threshold, extra gate charge is balanced by the inversion electrons, which respond exponentially to $\phi_s$, so the depletion layer stops growing. The depletion charge per area at threshold is $|Q'_{SD}(max)| = qN_ax_{dT}$.

study.title: Flat-band voltage
study.body:
Even at $V_G = 0$ the bands are usually bent, for two reasons:
- The gate and the substrate have different work functions. Measured from the oxide conduction band, $\phi_{ms} = \phi'_m - (\chi' + E_g/2q + \phi_{fp})$ for p-type Si (gate work function minus semiconductor work function). For an $n^+$ poly gate on p-type Si, $\phi_{ms} \approx -(E_g/2q + \phi_{fp})$; for a $p^+$ poly gate, $+(E_g/2q - \phi_{fp})$; for aluminium (with $\phi'_m$ = 3.20 V, $\chi'$ = 3.25 V), $-(0.61\ \text{V} + \phi_{fp})$.
- Positive charge trapped in the oxide near the interface, $Q'_{ss}$ (C/cm²), attracts electrons by itself.
The **flat-band voltage** undoes both:

study.title: Threshold voltage
study.body: At threshold the gate must (1) cancel $\phi_{ms}$ and the oxide charge ($V_{FB}$), (2) bend the bands by $2\phi_{fp}$, and (3) carry the depletion charge $|Q'_{SD}(max)|$ across the oxide capacitance. Higher doping or a thicker oxide raises $V_T$; positive oxide charge lowers it. For an n-type substrate (PMOS) all signs flip: $V_{TP} = -|Q'_{SD}|/C_{ox}$ $- Q'_{ss}/C_{ox}$ $+ \phi_{ms} - 2\phi_{fn}$.

study.title: Explore: the C–V curve
study.body: The small-signal capacitance is the oxide capacitance in series with the depletion capacitance $\varepsilon_s/x_d$. Accumulation: $C = C_{ox}$. Depletion: $C$ falls as $x_d$ grows. Beyond $V_T$ at **high frequency** (red) the inversion electrons cannot follow the signal, so $C$ stays at $C_{min}$; at **low frequency** (dashed) they can and $C$ returns to $C_{ox}$. $n^+$ poly gate, no oxide charge. The curves use the depletion approximation and an abrupt switch at $V_T$: real curves are rounded near $V_{FB}$, and the low-frequency curve climbs back to $C_{ox}$ gradually above $V_T$.

study.title: Oxide charge and the C–V curve
study.body: Fixed positive oxide charge $Q'_{ss}$ shifts the whole C–V curve to the **left** by $Q'_{ss}/C_{ox}$ without changing its shape: the gate needs less voltage because the oxide charge already attracts electrons. Measuring the shift of $V_{FB}$ against the ideal curve gives the oxide charge, a standard process check. Charges at the interface that can change state (interface traps) instead stretch the curve out.

steps.title: The MOS capacitor
steps.body: Gate, oxide, semiconductor: a parallel-plate capacitor whose bottom plate is the silicon surface. With a p-type substrate, a negative gate voltage attracts holes (**accumulation**), a positive one first pushes holes away (**depletion**) and then pulls electrons to the surface (**inversion**). The oxide capacitance per area sets how much charge a volt on the gate controls.

steps.prompt: Find the oxide capacitance per unit area for a {{t}} nm SiO$_2$ gate oxide. ($\varepsilon_{ox} = 3.9 \times 8.85\times10^{-14}$ F/cm)
Match each regime of a p-type MOS capacitor with what sits at the silicon surface
steps.explanation: A negative gate (relative to $V_{FB}$) attracts the majority holes. A moderately positive gate repels them, leaving ionized acceptors. A strongly positive gate attracts enough minority electrons to make the surface n-type. At $V_G = V_{FB}$ the semiconductor is neutral right up to the surface.

steps.title: Surface potential and threshold
steps.body: The band bending at the surface is the surface potential $\phi_s$. In the bulk of p-type Si, $E_F$ sits $q\phi_{fp}$ below $E_{Fi}$. When the bands bend down by $\phi_{fp}$ the surface is intrinsic; at $2\phi_{fp}$ it is as n-type as the bulk is p-type. That is the **threshold** of strong inversion.

steps.prompt: A MOS capacitor has a p-type substrate with $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³. Find the surface potential at threshold, $2\phi_{fp}$. ($kT/q$ = 0.0259 V)
Which band diagram (energy against depth, surface on the left) shows a p-type MOS capacitor in **inversion**? Red: $E_F$; dashed: $E_{Fi}$.
steps.explanation: In inversion the bands bend down so far that at the surface $E_{Fi}$ lies **below** $E_F$: there the electron concentration exceeds the hole concentration. Bending down a little (with $E_{Fi}$ still above $E_F$) is depletion, bending up is accumulation, and straight bands are flat band.

steps.prompt: A p-type MOS capacitor is driven into accumulation by a gate voltage above the flat-band voltage.
steps.explanation: Accumulation of holes needs a gate that is **negative** relative to $V_{FB}$: the negative gate charge attracts the positive holes. Gate voltages above $V_{FB}$ give depletion and, beyond $V_T$, inversion.

steps.title: Maximum depletion width
steps.body: Up to threshold the gate charge is balanced by uncovered acceptors in a layer of depth $x_d$. At threshold that layer is $x_{dT}$ deep; beyond it the inversion electrons take over. The depletion charge at threshold is $qN_ax_{dT}$ per unit area.

steps.prompt: Find the maximum depletion width $x_{dT}$ under the gate of a MOS capacitor on p-type Si with $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³. ($\varepsilon_s$ = 1.035$\times10^{-12}$ F/cm)
For $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³ the maximum depletion width is {{xdT*1e4||3}} µm. Find the depletion charge per area at threshold, $|Q'_{SD}(max)|$.
steps.explanation: $|Q'_{SD}(max)| = qN_ax_{dT}$ = 1.602$\times10^{-19}$ × {{Na}} × {{xdT}} cm = **{{1.602e-19*Na*xdT|C/cm²}}**. It grows roughly as $\sqrt{N_a}$.

steps.title: Flat band
steps.body: The work-function difference $\phi_{ms}$ between gate and substrate, and fixed positive charge $Q'_{ss}$ in the oxide, bend the bands even at $V_G = 0$. The flat-band voltage is the gate voltage that straightens them again. For an $n^+$ polysilicon gate on p-type Si, $\phi_{ms} \approx -(E_g/2q + \phi_{fp})$.

steps.prompt: An $n^+$ poly gate sits on {{t}} nm of oxide over p-type Si ($N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³). The oxide contains a fixed positive charge of {{Nss}} $q$/cm². Find the flat-band voltage.

steps.title: Threshold voltage
steps.body: To reach threshold the gate must first undo the flat-band offset, then bend the bands by $2\phi_{fp}$, and finally supply the voltage $|Q'_{SD}(max)|/C_{ox}$ that the depletion charge drops across the oxide.

steps.prompt: An NMOS capacitor has $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³, $t_{ox}$ = {{t}} nm, an $n^+$ poly gate and $Q'_{ss}/q$ = {{Nss}} cm$^{-2}$. Find the threshold voltage.
Fixed positive charge in the gate oxide makes the threshold voltage of an NMOS capacitor **more negative**.
steps.explanation: $V_{FB}$ contains $-Q'_{ss}/C_{ox}$: positive oxide charge already attracts electrons to the surface, so less gate voltage is needed. The whole C–V curve shifts to the left.

steps.prompt: Find the ratio $C_{min}/C_{ox}$ of the high-frequency C–V curve for $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³ and $t_{ox}$ = {{t}} nm.
steps.explanation: $x_{dT}$ = {{xdT*1e4||3}} µm. In series, $C'_{min} = \varepsilon_{ox}/(t_{ox} + (\varepsilon_{ox}/\varepsilon_s)x_{dT})$, so $C_{min}/C_{ox}$ = $t_{ox}/(t_{ox} + 0.333\,x_{dT})$ = {{t}} nm / ({{t}} nm + {{3.9/11.7*xdT*1e7||3}} nm) = **{{(t*1e-7)/(t*1e-7 + 3.9/11.7*xdT)||3}}**. A thin oxide or light doping gives a deep dip.

steps.prompt: The high-frequency C–V curve of an $n^+$-poly MOS capacitor ($N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³, $t_{ox}$ = {{t}} nm). Drag $V_G$ to the threshold voltage, where the capacitance stops falling.
steps.explanation: $\phi_{fp}$ = {{phi||3}} V, $V_{FB} = -(0.56 + \phi_{fp})$ = {{VFB||3}} V, $|Q'_{SD}|/C_{ox}$ = {{1.602e-19*Na*xdT/Cox||3}} V, so $V_T = V_{FB} + 2\phi_{fp} + |Q'_{SD}|/C_{ox}$ = **{{VT|V}}**. There the depletion layer reaches $x_{dT}$; above it the inversion electrons screen the substrate and the high-frequency capacitance stays at $C_{min}$.

steps.prompt: Why does the low-frequency C–V curve of a MOS capacitor rise back to $C_{ox}$ in strong inversion, while the high-frequency curve stays at $C_{min}$?
options: At low frequency, thermal generation can supply and remove inversion electrons in step with the signal; at high frequency it is too slow, so only the depletion edge responds
At high frequency the oxide capacitance decreases
At low frequency holes accumulate at the surface
At high frequency the depletion layer collapses
steps.explanation: The inversion layer is made of minority electrons, which must be generated thermally (or come from a nearby source region, as in a MOSFET). That takes milliseconds or more. A slow signal lets the charge change right at the surface (capacitance $C_{ox}$); a fast one forces the change to the depletion edge at $x_{dT}$ ($C_{min}$).

steps.prompt: At flat band the capacitance is set by the extrinsic Debye length $L_D = \sqrt{\varepsilon_s(kT/q)/(qN_a)}$: $C'_{FB} = \varepsilon_{ox}/(t_{ox} + (\varepsilon_{ox}/\varepsilon_s)L_D)$. Find $C'_{FB}/C_{ox}$ for $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³ and $t_{ox}$ = {{t}} nm.
steps.explanation: $L_D = \sqrt{\varepsilon_s(kT/q)/(qN_a)}$ = {{LD*1e7||3}} nm. $C'_{FB}/C_{ox} = t_{ox}/(t_{ox} + 0.333L_D)$ = {{t}} / ({{t}} + {{3.9/11.7*LD*1e7||3}}) = **{{(t*1e-7)/(t*1e-7 + 3.9/11.7*LD)||3}}**. The flat-band point is well below $C_{ox}$, which is how $V_{FB}$ is located on a measured curve.

steps.prompt: The dashed curve is the ideal high-frequency C–V curve of a p-type MOS capacitor, the solid one is measured. What does the shift tell you about the oxide?
options: It contains no charge; only $\phi_{ms}$ differs
steps.explanation: $\Delta V_{FB} = -Q'_{ss}/C_{ox}$. Here the measured curve is shifted by {{sh}} V (negative means to the left). A shift to the **left** means positive oxide charge: it already attracts electrons, so less gate voltage is needed. A shift to the right means negative charge. The work-function difference is already included in the ideal curve.

steps.prompt: A measured C–V curve is shifted {{dV}} V to the **left** of the ideal curve. The oxide is {{t}} nm thick. Find the fixed oxide charge density $Q'_{ss}/q$ in charges per cm² (answer in cm$^{-2}$).
steps.explanation: $Q'_{ss} = -C_{ox}\Delta V_{FB}$ with $\Delta V_{FB}$ = −{{dV}} V and $C_{ox}$ = {{3.4515e-13/(t*1e-7)|F/cm²}}: $Q'_{ss}$ = {{dV*3.4515e-13/(t*1e-7)|C/cm²}}. Dividing by $q$: **{{dV*3.4515e-13/(t*1e-7)/1.602e-19}}** cm$^{-2}$. Good modern oxides reach $10^{10}$ cm$^{-2}$ or less.

steps.prompt: A MOS capacitor on more heavily doped p-type silicon shows a **higher** minimum capacitance $C_{min}/C_{ox}$ (a shallower dip).
steps.explanation: $x_{dT} = \sqrt{4\varepsilon_s\phi_{fp}/qN_a}$ shrinks with doping (the $\ln N_a$ in $\phi_{fp}$ grows only slowly), so the depletion capacitance at threshold is larger and $C_{min}$ rises towards $C_{ox}$.

steps.prompt: An NMOS process uses an $n^+$ poly gate, $t_{ox}$ = {{t}} nm and no oxide charge. Drag the substrate doping until the threshold voltage is {{VTt||3}} V (dashed line).
steps.explanation: $V_T = |Q'_{SD}|/C_{ox}$ $- (0.56 + \phi_{fp}) + 2\phi_{fp}$ must equal {{VTt||3}} V, which happens at $N_a$ ≈ **{{Nt}} cm⁻³** ($\phi_{fp}$ = {{phiT||3}} V, $|Q'_{SD}|/C_{ox}$ = {{sqrt(4*1.602e-19*1.03545e-12*Nt*phiT)/Cox||3}} V). In practice the threshold is set with a shallow channel implant rather than the whole substrate doping.

steps.prompt: A PMOS capacitor has an n-type substrate ($N_d$ = {{Nd}} cm⁻³), $t_{ox}$ = {{t}} nm, a $p^+$ poly gate ($\phi_{ms} = +(0.56 + \phi_{fn})$) and no oxide charge. Find $V_{TP} = -|Q'_{SD}(max)|/C_{ox}$ $+ \phi_{ms} - 2\phi_{fn}$.
steps.explanation: $\phi_{fn} = (kT/q)\ln(N_d/n_i)$ = {{phi||3}} V; $|Q'_{SD}|$ = {{Q|C/cm²}}, $C_{ox}$ = {{Cox|F/cm²}}, so $|Q'_{SD}|/C_{ox}$ = {{Q/Cox||3}} V. $\phi_{ms}$ = {{0.56+phi||3}} V. $V_{TP}$ = −{{Q/Cox||3}} + {{0.56+phi||3}} − {{2*phi||3}} = **{{-Q/Cox + (0.56 + phi) - 2*phi||3}} V**. Mirror image of the NMOS case: a $p^+$ gate gives a PMOS threshold of the same size as an $n^+$ gate gives NMOS.

steps.prompt: An aluminium gate ($\phi'_m$ = 3.20 V) sits on SiO$_2$ over p-type Si ($\chi'$ = 3.25 V, $E_g$ = 1.12 eV) with $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³. Find $\phi_{ms} = \phi'_m - (\chi' + E_g/2q + \phi_{fp})$.

Above threshold every extra volt on the gate adds inversion charge $Q'_n = -C_{ox}(V_G - V_T)$. For $t_{ox}$ = {{t}} nm and $V_G - V_T$ = {{Vov}} V, how many electrons per cm² are in the channel? (answer in cm$^{-2}$)
steps.explanation: $|Q'_n| = C_{ox}(V_G - V_T)$ = {{3.4515e-13/(t*1e-7)|F/cm²}} × {{Vov}} V = {{3.4515e-13/(t*1e-7)*Vov|C/cm²}}. Divide by $q$: **{{3.4515e-13/(t*1e-7)*Vov/1.602e-19}}** cm$^{-2}$. This sheet charge is what carries the MOSFET current in the next unit; a thinner oxide gives more charge per volt.

steps.prompt: Put the steps to calculate the depletion-charge term and the threshold voltage of an NMOS capacitor in order
items: Use $\phi_{fp}$ to find the maximum depletion width $x_{dT}$
Divide by $C_{ox}$ to get the voltage across the oxide
steps.explanation: Each step needs the result of the one before: $\phi_{fp}$ sets $x_{dT} = \sqrt{4\varepsilon_s\phi_{fp}/qN_a}$, which gives the depletion charge $qN_ax_{dT}$; $C_{ox}$ converts that charge into a voltage, and adding $V_{FB} = \phi_{ms} - Q'_{ss}/C_{ox}$ and the band bending $2\phi_{fp}$ gives $V_T$.

steps.prompt: The gate oxide of an NMOS capacitor is made {{k}} times thinner, everything else unchanged (no oxide charge). Which term of $V_T$ changes?
steps.explanation: $C_{ox} = \varepsilon_{ox}/t_{ox}$ grows {{k}}-fold, so the depletion-charge term $|Q'_{SD}|/C_{ox}$ drops {{k}}-fold. $\phi_{ms}$ and $2\phi_{fp}$ depend only on the materials and doping. (With oxide charge, the $Q'_{ss}/C_{ox}$ term shrinks too.)

steps.prompt: An aluminium-gate NMOS capacitor ($\phi_{ms} = -(0.61\ \text{V} + \phi_{fp})$) has $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³, $t_{ox}$ = {{t}} nm and $Q'_{ss}/q$ = {{Nss}} cm$^{-2}$. Find $V_{TN}$.
An NMOS capacitor with an $n^+$ poly gate, a 10 nm oxide, no oxide charge and $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³ is already in inversion at $V_G$ = 0.
